title: God comes down without changing
source_text: Ἴδωμεν δὲ καὶ ἅπερ ἑξῆς φησιν ὁ Κέλσος μετὰ μεγάλης ἀπαγγελίας τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον· ἔτι δὲ, φησὶν, ἄνωθεν πλείοσιν ἀποδείξεσιν ἀναλάβωμεν τὸν λόγον, λέγω δὲ οὐδὲν καινὸν ἀλλὰ πάλαι δεδογμένα, ὁ θεὸς ἀγαθός ἐστι καὶ καλὸς καὶ εὐδαίμων καὶ ἐν τῷ καλλίστῳ καὶ ἀρίστῳ· εἰ δὴ ἐς ἀνθρώπους κάτεισι, μεταβολῆς αὐτῷ δεῖ, μεταβολῆς δὲ ἐξ ἀγαθοῦ εἰς κακὸν καὶ ἐκ καλοῦ εἰς αἰσχρὸν καὶ ἐξ εὐδαιμονίας εἰς κακοδαιμονίαν καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ἀρίστου εἰς τὸ πονηρότατον, τίς ἄν οὖν ἕλοιτο τοιαύτην μεταβολήν; καὶ μὲν δὴ τῷ θνητῷ μὲν ἀλλάττεσθαι καὶ μεταπλάττεσθαι φύσις, τῷ δ᾿ ἀθανάτῳ κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως ἔχειν, οὐκ ἂν οὖν οὐδὲ ταύτην τὴν μεταβολὴν θεὸς δέχοιτο, δοκεῖ δή μοι πρὸς ταῦτα λέγεσθαι τὰ δέοντα διηγησαμένῳ τὴν ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς λεγομένην κατάβασιν θεοῦ πρὸς τὰ ἀνθρώπινα· εἰς ἣν οὐ μεταβολῆς αὐτῷ δεῖ, ὡς Κέλσος οἴεται ἡμᾶς λέγειν, οὔτε τροπῆς τῆς ἐξ ἀγαθοῦ εἰς κακὸν ἢ ἐκ καλοῦ εἰς αἰσχρὸν ἢ ἐξ εὐδαιμονίας εἰς κακοδαιμονίαν ἢ ἐκ τοῦ ἀρίστου εἰς τὸ πονηρότατον, μένων γὰρ τῇ οὐσίᾳ ἄτρεπτος συγκαταβαίνει τῇ προνοίᾳ καὶ τῇ οἰκονομίᾳ τοῖς ἀνθρωπίνοις πράγμασιν, ἡμεῖς μὲν οὖν καὶ τὰ θεῖα γράμματα παρίσταμεν ἄτρεπτον λέγοντα τὸν θεὸν ἔν τε τῷ „σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ“ καὶ ἐν τῷ „οὐκ ἠλλοίωμαι“· οἱ δὲ τοῦ Ἐπικούρου θεοὶ, σύνθετοι ἐξ ἀτόμων τυγχάνοντες καὶ τὸ ὅσον ἐπὶ τῇ συστάσει ἀναλυτοὶ, πραγματεύονται τὰς φθοροποιοὺς ἀτόμους ἀποσείεσθαι,· ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ τῶν Στωϊκῶν θεὸς, ἅτε σῶμα τυγχάνων, ὁτὲ μὲν ἡγεμονικὸν ἔχει τὴν ὅλην οὐσίαν, ὅταν ἡ ἐκπύρωσις ᾖ· ὁτὲ δὲ ἐπὶ μέρους γίνεται αὐτῆς, ὅταν ᾖ διακόσμησις. οὐδὲ γὰρ δεδύνηνται οὗτοι τρανῶσαι τὴν φυσικὴν τοῦ θεοῦ ἔννοιαν ὡς πάντῃ ἀφθάρτου καὶ ἁπλοῦ καὶ ἀσυνθέτου καὶ ἀδιαιρέτου.
pass_a_gloss: Let us see (ἴδωμεν) also what Celsus says next with great announcement (μετὰ μεγάλης ἀπαγγελίας) in this manner: 'Further, let us take up (ἀναλάβωμεν) the argument from above/afresh (ἄνωθεν) with more demonstrations (ἀποδείξεσιν); I say nothing new (καινόν) but things long held (πάλαι δεδογμένα): God is good (ἀγαθός) and beautiful (καλός) and happy (εὐδαίμων) and in the most beautiful and best (ἐν τῷ καλλίστῳ καὶ ἀρίστῳ). If then he comes down (κάτεισι) to men, he needs change (μεταβολῆς δεῖ), change from good to bad (κακόν), from beautiful to shameful (αἰσχρόν), from happiness to unhappiness (κακοδαιμονία), from best to most wicked (πονηρότατον). Who would choose (ἕλοιτο) such a change? And indeed to the mortal it is nature (φύσις) to be altered (ἀλλάττεσθαι) and remoulded (μεταπλάττεσθαι), but to the immortal to be in the same respects and alike (κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως ἔχειν). So God would not accept (δέχοιτο) this change either.' It seems to me the needful things are said against this by one who has narrated (διηγησαμένῳ) the descent (κατάβασις) of God to human things spoken of in the Scriptures; for which he needs no change, as Celsus thinks we say, nor turning (τροπή) from good to bad ... For remaining unchangeable (ἄτρεπτος) in essence (οὐσίᾳ) he comes down with/condescends (συγκαταβαίνει) by providence (προνοίᾳ) and dispensation (οἰκονομίᾳ) to human affairs. We then present the divine writings (θεῖα γράμματα) too as calling God unchangeable, in 'but you are the same' and in 'I have not been altered (οὐκ ἠλλοίωμαι)'. But the gods of Epicurus, being composite (σύνθετοι) from atoms and, as far as their constitution (σύστασις) goes, dissoluble (ἀναλυτοί), labour (πραγματεύονται) to shake off (ἀποσείεσθαι) the destruction-making (φθοροποιούς) atoms; and the god of the Stoics, being a body (σῶμα), at one time has the whole substance as ruling part, when there is conflagration, at another comes to be in part of it, when there is world-ordering. For they have not been able to make plain the natural notion of God as wholly incorruptible, simple, uncompounded, indivisible.

lemmas.lemma: κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως ἔχειν

pass_b_english: Let us look also at what Celsus says next, with a grand announcement, in this way: “Further,” he says, “let us take up the argument again from the beginning with more proofs. I say nothing new, only what has long been settled. God is good and beautiful and happy, and is in what is most beautiful and best. If, then, he comes down to men, he must undergo change: a change from good to bad, from beautiful to shameful, from happiness to misery, and from what is best to what is most wicked. Who would choose such a change? Besides, it is the nature of what is mortal to be altered and remoulded, but of what is immortal to remain the same and unchanging. So God would not accept this change either.”

To this, it seems to me, the needful answer is given by explaining what the Scriptures say about the descent of God to human affairs. For this he needs no change, as Celsus thinks we say, nor any turning from good to bad, or from beautiful to shameful, or from happiness to misery, or from what is best to what is most wicked. For, remaining unchangeable in his essence, he comes down to human affairs by his providence and his ordering of things.

We, then, show that the divine writings also speak of God as unchangeable, both in the words “But you are the same” (Psalm 102:27) and in “I have not changed” (Malachi 3:6). But the gods of Epicurus, being made up of atoms and, so far as their structure goes, liable to dissolve, are busy shaking off the atoms that would destroy them. And the god of the Stoics too, since he is a body, at one time has the whole of substance as his ruling part, when the conflagration takes place, and at another comes to be in a part of it, when the world is set in order. For these men have not been able to bring out clearly the natural conception of God as in every way incorruptible, simple, uncompounded and indivisible.

choices.choice: 'abides in' -> 'is in' (Greek has only ἐν; 'abides' added sense and sounded archaic)
'could not accept' -> 'would not accept' (potential optative δέχοιτο; modality fixed)
'the descent of God to human affairs of which the Scriptures speak' -> 'what the Scriptures say about the descent of God to human affairs' (λεγομένην modifies κατάβασιν, not 'human affairs')
moved 'to human affairs' before 'by his providence' for natural English order

Celsus's quotation runs from 'Further' to 'either'; the attribution 'he says' is kept where the Greek places it. 'σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ' is LXX Psalm 101:28 = English Psalm 102:27. 'οὐκ ἠλλοίωμαι' = Malachi 3:6 LXX. Celsus's 'κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως ἔχειν' is Platonic wording (compare Phaedo 78c-d, Statesman 269d) and the argument that a god will not change for the worse echoes Republic 2, 380d-381c; not cited inline because Celsus does not quote a single passage verbatim. 'οὐκ ἂν ... δέχοιτο' is a potential optative: 'would not accept'. 'συγκαταβαίνει τῇ προνοίᾳ καὶ τῇ οἰκονομίᾳ' rendered 'comes down by his providence and his ordering of things'; συγκατάβασις carries the sense of accommodating descent. Stoic terms: ἡγεμονικόν = ruling part, ἐκπύρωσις = conflagration, διακόσμησις = ordered world-arrangement.
